articles.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
articles.text:
Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
- Date:
- November 19, 2026
- Source:
- University of Tokyo
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.
- Share:
Deep beneath the ocean's surface, strange, translucent creatures known as sea pigs crawl across the seafloor. Now, researchers at the University of Tokyo have discovered that these unusual animals are hiding something even stranger beneath their "skin." Living within their body walls is a previously unknown bacterium with an extraordinarily small genome and a surprising collection of genes responsible for producing enormous proteins.
The researchers identified the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola, and used fluorescence imaging to pinpoint its location inside sea pig tissues. Genetic analysis revealed that its genome contains just 649,000 DNA bases, yet more than a quarter of its genetic material is devoted to producing groups of proteins associated with the bacterial surface. Some of these "giant" proteins contain more than 5,000 amino acids and may help the bacteria interact with their hosts or form clusters (clustering into groups). The discovery offers new insights into how bacteria adapt to living in close association with other organisms and which biological functions they retain as they become increasingly dependent on their hosts.
Meet the Strange Sea Pigs of the Deep Ocean
Sea lions, seahorses, and sea cows may be familiar marine animals, but sea pigs are considerably less well known. These small, gelatinous creatures are actually a type of sea cucumber that inhabits the deep ocean. Using numerous tube-shaped feet, they slowly travel across the seafloor, gathering decaying organic material and delivering it to their mouths with specialized tentacles.
Despite their unusual appearance, sea pigs perform important work in the deep-sea ecosystem. By consuming dead organic matter, they help recycle nutrients that support other marine life. Their soft, seemingly vulnerable bodies also provide an unexpected benefit to other animals. Young king crabs have been observed using sea pigs as shelter from predators.
Many aspects of sea pig biology, however, remain mysterious. Researchers still do not know how long these animals live or precisely why they have long, waving projections resembling antennae on their heads. Another important unanswered question concerns the bacteria that inhabit the layers beneath their outer surfaces.
Sea pigs belong to a group of marine invertebrates called echinoderms (marine invertebrates including sea cucumbers and sea stars). Like other members of this group, they can harbor bacteria beneath their outer body covering. Scientists are particularly interested in understanding how these microorganisms interact with their hosts and how such relationships evolved. This research is also ecologically important because sea cucumbers make up more than 90% of the biomass of large seafloor animals in some deep-ocean environments.
"Taxonomic and genomic information about these body-wall inhabiting bacteria is scarce, and very few studies of deep-sea species have linked this information to the bacteria's location within host tissues," said Yu Yoshida, a Ph.D. student at the University of Tokyo's Graduate School of Frontier Sciences and a lead author of the study.
Scientists Discover a Dominant Bacterium Beneath Sea Pig Skin
To investigate these hidden microorganisms, researchers from several Japanese institutions, including the University of Tokyo, examined eight sea pigs collected during deep-sea research expeditions.
The team extracted DNA from different tissues to identify the bacteria present throughout the animals' bodies. They also reconstructed the genomes of the most abundant bacterial groups, allowing them to investigate their genetic characteristics. Finally, they used fluorescence imaging, a technique that makes selected biological structures visible through fluorescent signals, to determine precisely where the bacteria lived within the sea pig tissues.
The results revealed that one particular bacterium was remarkably abundant in the animals' body walls.
"What we found was that in body-wall samples from the three sea pig species, one bacterium accounted for more than 70% of bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences (a genetic marker used in identifying bacteria), so it truly dominated the body wall," explained Yoshida.
Further investigation showed that this dominant bacterium belongs to a broader group of microorganisms known to live in close association with marine invertebrates. However, its genetic characteristics differ substantially from those of previously identified members of that group.
Because of these differences, the researchers have proposed recognizing Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola as a new bacterial genus and species.
A Tiny Genome Packed With Giant Proteins
One of the most surprising findings emerged when the scientists examined the bacterium's DNA. Its genome was exceptionally compact, containing only 649,000 bases, the chemical units that make up genetic material.
By comparison, the genome of Escherichia coli, a widely studied bacterium commonly found in the intestines of humans and other animals, is roughly seven times larger.
"The complete genome was very small, only 649,000 bases. By comparison, the E. coli genome is approximately seven times larger. However, we were more surprised by the composition. Genes for some of the energy-generating pathways (used for breaking down nutrients and generating energy) which are commonly found in bacteria were not detected," explained Yoshida.
The absence of genes involved in certain energy-producing processes suggests that the bacterium may have lost some of the biological machinery that many other bacteria use to survive independently.
Yet even more remarkable was how much of its limited genetic material was devoted to proteins associated with its surface.
"Meanwhile, genes for encoding surface-associated protein groups (that is, DNA with the blueprints for building specific proteins on cell surfaces) accounted for 27.6% of the entire genome. This included genes for proteins exceeding 5,000 amino acids. As bacterial proteins average about 300 amino acids in length, 5,000 is exceptionally long. This offers us important clues as to which functions are retained in bacteria which live in close association with their host."
Proteins are built from chains of amino acids, and their structures help determine the jobs they perform. The unusually large proteins identified in this bacterium could be involved in interactions with sea pig tissues or in helping bacterial cells stick together. Their exact functions remain unknown.
The discovery suggests that, as the bacterium evolved to depend more heavily on its host, it may have retained certain specialized capabilities while losing genes needed for other essential processes.
What Do Sea Pigs Gain From These Mysterious Bacteria?
The bacterium's unusually reduced genome offers an important clue about its lifestyle. Researchers believe Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola relies extensively on its sea pig host to obtain substances it cannot adequately produce for itself.
These include amino acids, which are necessary for building proteins, along with nucleic acid precursors, lipids, and mineral nutrients. Nucleic acid precursors are the molecular building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, while lipids are important components of cell membranes and other cellular structures.
Because the bacterium lacks some of the genes needed to produce or process essential compounds independently, living within the sea pig's tissues may provide access to resources required for its survival.
What remains unclear is whether the relationship also benefits the sea pig. One possibility is that the bacteria help defend their hosts against pathogens, potentially offering protection from disease-causing microorganisms. However, the researchers emphasize that this potential benefit has not yet been demonstrated.
Understanding why this particular bacterium becomes so abundant in sea pig body walls is another major question. Scientists also hope to determine what its unusually large surface proteins do, how it competes with other microorganisms, and whether its presence changes the health or biology of its host.
"We would really like to understand how this bacterium could become so dominant in the body wall, the functions of the giant surface proteins, what competition it faces from other bacteria, and of course the effects on the host," said Yoshida. "More broadly, further investigation could provide fundamental insights into how bacteria colonize hosts and adopt a host-dependent lifestyle."
The findings highlight how much remains to be discovered about life in the deep ocean. By investigating the microscopic organisms living within these unusual animals, scientists hope to better understand the evolutionary processes that allow bacteria to form intimate, long-lasting relationships with their hosts.

articles.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
articles.text:
Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
- Date:
- November 19, 2026
- Source:
- Adelaide University
- Summary:
- Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.
- Share:
Hydrogen flames can glow bright orange one day and become almost impossible to see the next, even when the burner settings remain exactly the same. Researchers at Adelaide University have now identified a surprising reason for this dramatic change, offering insights that could help make hydrogen-powered stoves, ovens, and other household appliances safer and more dependable.
The study, published in Next Energy, found that much of the difference comes down to sodium, a naturally occurring element carried through the air in microscopic particles. Sea salt transported inland by the wind is one important source.
When sodium is present in the surrounding air, hydrogen flames can take on a noticeable orange glow. But when sodium concentrations fall, the flames become much harder to see, even though the burner continues operating under the same conditions.
This discovery has important implications for the development of hydrogen appliances. Instead of depending on flame color to show whether a burner is running, engineers may need to incorporate other detection technologies. Improving these systems could help support the adoption of hydrogen as a lower-emissions alternative to natural gas.
Why Hydrogen Flames Change Color With the Weather
Lead researcher Professor Paul Medwell, from the School of Electrical and Mechanical Engineering at Adelaide University, explained that studying hydrogen flames under ordinary environmental conditions is essential for developing appliances that people can safely and confidently use at home.*
"Hydrogen has significant potential as part of a lower-emissions energy future, and we need to understand how it behaves in the real world if we want people to be confident using it.
"Our research helps explain why hydrogen flames can look different from one day to the next. That knowledge gives engineers valuable information to develop appliances and flame-detection systems that work reliably, regardless of changing environmental conditions."
To investigate these changes, the researchers combined controlled laboratory experiments with outdoor testing around Adelaide. They examined how hydrogen flames responded to variations in atmospheric conditions, including shifting weather patterns and changes in the air reaching the burner.
Over two weeks, the team monitored light emissions from hydrogen flames while keeping the burner settings unchanged. Despite the consistent operating conditions, the sodium-related light signal varied by more than 28 times between its lowest and highest recorded values.
Weather played a major role in those differences. Air that had passed over the ocean generally contained more sodium, producing flames with a stronger orange glow. When the air carried less sodium, the flames appeared considerably fainter.
Hydrogen Flames Are Harder to See Than Natural Gas Flames
The researchers also examined how hydrogen flames compared with those produced by a conventional natural gas cooktop.
They found that hydrogen flames emitted less visible light on average, even when atmospheric conditions favored a brighter flame. This difference presents an additional challenge for appliances that use visible flames to indicate whether a burner is operating.
Hydrogen combustion can also produce faint blue and red light. However, the researchers found that these colors were easiest to detect in darkened surroundings, making them less useful as reliable visual indicators under everyday lighting conditions.
Together, the findings show why judging whether a hydrogen burner is operating based on appearance alone may be unreliable. A flame that is clearly visible under one set of conditions could become extremely difficult to detect when the surrounding air changes.
Making Hydrogen-Powered Homes Safer
Medwell emphasized that the results do not undermine hydrogen's potential as an energy source. Instead, they demonstrate why appliances must be engineered to accommodate the fuel's particular properties.
"Different energy sources have different properties, and good engineering is about understanding those differences and designing for them.
"Rather than relying on a flame looking a particular color, we can investigate other ways of confirming that a burner is operating. Options include specialized ultraviolet or infrared flame detectors and temperature sensors.
"By identifying the factors that influence flame visibility, we can help inform the development of hydrogen appliances that are fit for purpose in real homes and other everyday settings."
Such detection systems could provide a more dependable way to confirm that hydrogen is burning, regardless of whether its flame appears orange, faint blue, or is barely visible.
By identifying how environmental sodium affects flame visibility, the research provides information that engineers can use when designing hydrogen appliances for kitchens and other everyday environments. That knowledge could help make the technology safer and more practical as interest in lower-emissions energy alternatives grows.
The project brought together researchers from Adelaide University, the University of New South Wales, and Gas Infrastructure Research Australia. Support came through the Future Fuels Cooperative Research Centre, with funding provided under the Australian Government's Cooperative Research Centres Program.
The study, 'The role of sodium on hydrogen flame visibility in domestic settings,' was published in Next Energy
*In 2023, the Australian Gas Infrastructure Group (AGIG) introduced Australia's first 100% hydrogen-powered home in Victoria. The demonstration showed that household gas appliances could operate entirely on hydrogen, a development described as a 'game changer'.

articles.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
articles.text:
Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
- Date:
- November 19, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.
- Share:
As temperatures rise, the floating ice shelves that help hold Antarctica's massive ice sheet in place are melting and breaking apart at record rates. As these protective barriers disappear, they expose towering walls of solid ice. Whether these cliffs remain standing or collapse could play a major role in Antarctica's future ice loss and its contribution to rising sea levels worldwide.
For years, scientists have believed that ice cliffs become unstable once they exceed 100 meters in height, roughly as tall as the Statue of Liberty. According to this theory, a cliff that grows too tall will collapse under its own weight, exposing an even taller wall of ice farther inland. That new cliff would then collapse, potentially setting off a chain reaction that causes the ice sheet to retreat rapidly.
But new research from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) challenges this long-standing assumption. The findings suggest that the fate of an Antarctic ice cliff depends on much more than its height, and that even dramatic collapses do not necessarily lead to an unstoppable retreat.
Published in the journal Science, the study examined satellite observations of more than 15,000 Antarctic ice cliffs collected over four years. Researchers discovered a surprising pattern: When the cliffs collapsed, they sometimes retreated much faster than existing models predicted. Yet rather than continuing to disintegrate, the affected glaciers soon stabilized.
"We found that when the cliffs were retreating, they were doing so faster than what has been modeled, which would mean more ice loss and higher contributions of sea level rise," says study author Caroline Needell, a graduate student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program. "But because we found that the retreat was short-lived, and all the glaciers eventually stabilized, that would suggest that things won't be so bad. We don't see this runaway effect."
The study's co-authors are Catherine Walker, an assistant scientist at WHOI, and Jeremy Bassis, an associate professor at the University of Michigan.
Why Scientists Expected Antarctica's Ice Cliffs to Collapse
The possibility of runaway ice cliff collapse is described by a theory called marine ice cliff instability (MICI). It proposes that when an exposed ice wall reaches a critical height, its own weight makes it structurally unstable. If the cliff falls and reveals an even taller wall behind it, the process could repeat, progressively eating away at the Antarctic ice sheet.
Earlier research investigated this possibility primarily through computer models. Scientists used the physical properties of ice to estimate how enormous frozen cliffs should behave, then compared those calculations with a limited number of observations from Antarctica. These studies suggested that cliffs taller than approximately 100 meters were particularly vulnerable to collapse.
"Predictive ice-sheet models that have been used so far to represent ice cliff instability just take into account cliff height," Needell notes. "That's the only variable that matters. And once the cliff height reaches the critical threshold, usually 100 meters, it should initiate this runaway effect of ice sheet retreat."
Needell and her colleagues wanted to test those predictions against a much larger collection of real-world measurements. They sought to determine how tall Antarctica's ice cliffs actually become and whether their collapse consistently triggers the destructive chain reactions predicted by existing models.
Satellites Reveal Surprising Ice Cliff Stability
To investigate, the researchers turned to NASA's Ice, Cloud, and Land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2). This spacecraft repeatedly travels over Earth's polar regions, using a laser-based instrument called an altimeter to measure elevations with great precision. Its observations track the heights of glaciers, ice sheets, and sea ice, as well as ocean levels in and around Antarctica.
The team analyzed measurements gathered between 2019 and 2023, examining more than 15,000 ice cliffs at three-month intervals. Most were far shorter than the height considered dangerous by earlier models. The average cliff stood approximately 30 meters tall, although a small number exceeded the proposed 100-meter instability threshold.
The researchers also searched for characteristics that might explain why some cliffs remained stable while others retreated.
One important clue came from the broken ice accumulating in front of the cliffs. Known as mélange, this material consists of a slushy mixture of sea ice and fragments of icebergs. Cliffs that remained relatively stationary tended to have thicker accumulations of mélange, suggesting that the debris could help support the towering ice walls.
"We measured mélange height and found taller cliffs have thicker mélange, which could be a built-in stabilizing effect," Needell explains.
Surrounding seawater provided another possible source of stability. The observations indicated that deeper water can exert greater supporting pressure against an ice cliff, helping counteract the forces that might otherwise cause it to collapse.
Together, these findings suggest that the stability of Antarctica's ice cliffs cannot be predicted by height alone. Conditions in the water surrounding the ice may also determine whether a cliff remains standing.
Antarctica's Tallest Ice Cliffs Collapse, Then Stabilize
"After we did that global analysis, we thought, ok, let's zoom in on the tallest cliffs and see how they're behaving," Needell says.
The researchers selected four locations around Antarctica where satellites had recorded some of the tallest ice cliffs. Each stood approximately 100 meters high, with the tallest reaching 127 meters. The team then reconstructed how these cliffs changed at three-month intervals throughout the four-year study.
The results initially appeared to support the idea that extremely tall cliffs are unstable. These towering walls did collapse, and the glaciers behind them retreated at speeds substantially greater than those anticipated by existing MICI models.
However, the retreat did not continue indefinitely.
"But that retreat was short-lived," Needell notes.
Instead of retreating farther inland in a continuous series of collapses, the glaciers stabilized and eventually advanced outward toward the ocean again.
"It's this rapid retreat, punctuated by periods of stabilization," Needell says. "That was puzzling to us. Then, we thought: We need to look at all the things that affect cliff height."
The unexpected pattern suggested that some overlooked physical processes were interrupting the collapse before it could develop into a sustained chain reaction.
Hidden Ridges Beneath the Ice Act as Natural Speed Bumps
To understand what was stopping the retreat, the team examined the shape of the land beneath Antarctica's ice sheet.
This underlying terrain, known as bed topography, can strongly influence the height and stability of the ice above it. When the ground is relatively flat, the visible slope of the ice more closely reflects the thickness of the ice itself. But when the terrain rises into a ridge or bump, the ice resting on that elevated ground is thinner than its overall surface elevation might suggest.
These buried rises can function like natural speed bumps. By reducing the thickness of the overlying ice, they can make exposed cliffs shorter and less vulnerable to collapse.
When the scientists compared the locations of stabilizing ice cliffs with measurements of Antarctica's underlying terrain, they found that the cliffs frequently stopped retreating where the ground rose beneath them.
The researchers identified another important process. Taller cliffs tended to "thin out" more rapidly as they collapsed. Rather than remaining towering, unstable walls, they could quickly shrink into shorter cliffs that were better able to withstand further collapse.
These effects help explain why the researchers observed rapid initial ice loss followed by periods of stability, rather than the continuous retreat anticipated by earlier models.
What the Discovery Means for Future Sea Level Rise
The findings could help scientists improve predictions of how Antarctica's ice sheet will respond to continued warming.
Although the researchers observed some cliffs collapsing faster than expected, the rapid retreat was temporary in the locations they studied. This challenges the assumption that crossing a particular height threshold inevitably leads to runaway collapse.
The results do not mean Antarctica's ice sheet is safe from further losses. Instead, they reveal that predicting its future requires accounting for several interacting factors, including the shape of the land beneath the ice, the rate at which ice becomes thinner, the depth of surrounding water, and the stabilizing effects of broken ice.
"Now we know what to look for," Needell says. "We really need to know the bed topography, and we need to know the ice thinning rate, in order to get ice cliff instability right, because this value really matters in the context of projecting sea level rise."
By incorporating these additional processes into ice sheet models, scientists may be able to produce more reliable estimates of Antarctica's future contribution to global sea level rise.

articles.title: Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?
articles.text:
Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?
- Date:
- November 19, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Why do Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others? Scientists are investigating whether the body's hidden energy-saving response could help explain the difference and unlock more effective, personalized weight-loss treatments.
- Share:
Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.
Research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite.
These medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time.
We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially important piece in a complex puzzle.
The challenge of metabolic adaptation
Research has shown semaglutide medications to improve quality of life, blood markers such as sugar or cholesterol, strength and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work.
We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age and sex.
Energy metabolism may also be an important piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym and the everyday act of digesting food.
When we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis.
Think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau.
Emerging areas of research
Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an important role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories.
Researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term.
We published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization. We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive.
The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study, and remains an open question for exploration.
Personalized approaches to obesity
At the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter. This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use. This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating and during exercise.
We are currently recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation issues, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition, and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches.
Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an important step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment.
This will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey.
Lifestyle changes for success
Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes.

articles.title: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search
articles.text:
Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search
- Date:
- November 18, 2026
- Source:
- Aberystwyth University
- Summary:
- A major new investigation into Stonehenge’s mysterious six-ton Altar Stone has uncovered fresh clues while ruling out several suspected sources. Once thought to have originated in Wales, the massive sandstone slab is now believed to have come from northeastern Scotland, although researchers have yet to find an exact match.
- Share:
The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.
A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.
Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.
Now, a new international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.
New Geological Clues Narrow the Search
To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.
Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.
The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.
Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.
Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:
"This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer."
From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned
For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.
The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.
Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, said:
"For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries."
Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the new investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.
Solving Stonehenge's Six-Ton Mystery
Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.
Stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.
If the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.
Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:
"In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."
The researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.
The international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer
articles.text:
Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer
- Date:
- November 18, 2026
- Source:
- University of British Columbia
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a rare inherited mutation in the CDK12 gene linked to aggressive prostate cancer, with all five identified carriers developing metastatic disease between ages 44 and 62. The finding could lead to expanded genetic testing, helping families uncover hidden cancer risks and potentially detect the disease while it is still treatable.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a previously unrecognized inherited form of prostate cancer that, although extremely rare, can lead to aggressive disease relatively early in life. The discovery, made by researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC), could help doctors identify families with a heightened genetic risk and detect cancer before it spreads.
Most cancers develop as genetic changes build up in cells over time. However, approximately 5% to 10% are associated with inherited mutations that can be passed from parents to their children, creating a cancer risk that may extend across generations.
Among the most familiar examples are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These inherited changes can substantially raise the likelihood of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. Testing for BRCA mutations has reshaped cancer prevention and treatment by allowing people with elevated risks to receive earlier screening and preventive care.
Now, a study published in Cancer Discovery points to another gene, CDK12, as a potentially important marker of inherited prostate cancer risk. After examining genetic information from more than 4,500 people with aggressive prostate cancer, the researchers discovered five unrelated men with inherited mutations in CDK12. Every one of these men developed metastatic prostate cancer between ages 44 and 62, meaning the cancer had spread beyond the prostate.
"What's striking is that every patient we identified with this inherited mutation had already developed metastatic disease by the time they were diagnosed," said senior author Dr. Alexander Wyatt, associate professor of urologic sciences in the UBC faculty of medicine and UBC President's Excellence Chair in Precision Oncology. "The opportunity now is to identify these families earlier and give people the chance to benefit from enhanced screening, when there are still curative treatment options."
A Hidden Genetic Cause of Aggressive Prostate Cancer
The discovery challenges a longstanding assumption about CDK12. Scientists previously believed that harmful changes in this gene developed spontaneously inside cancer cells rather than being inherited from a parent.
To investigate whether the inherited mutations were actually contributing to the disease, the team examined the patients' tumors for a distinctive pattern of genetic damage associated with loss of CDK12 function. This molecular fingerprint helped connect the inherited mutations to the development of their cancers.
"The tumors provided us with a genetic signature that pointed directly back to CDK12," said lead author Dr. Sofie Tolmeijer, a postdoctoral fellow in the Wyatt lab. "It gave us compelling evidence that these inherited mutations were playing a direct role in causing their cancer."
The findings emerged from a broad international research effort involving UBC, BC Cancer, the Vancouver Coastal Health Research Institute, and the University of Washington, along with scientists at institutions in Australia, the Netherlands, Spain, and Belgium.
Despite the potentially serious consequences, inherited CDK12 mutations appear to be exceptionally uncommon. The researchers found them in approximately one out of every 1,000 people with aggressive prostate cancer. Even at that low frequency, they estimate that hundreds of families around the world could be affected.
"While this mutation is extremely rare, the discovery could be lifesaving for the families who carry it," said Dr. Tolmeijer. "Finding one person with an inherited mutation gives us the opportunity to identify other family members at risk and help them take action before cancer develops or spreads."
Genetic Testing Could Help Detect Prostate Cancer Earlier
One of the most promising implications of the discovery is that doctors may not need to develop entirely new testing technology to put the findings into practice.
The researchers recommend including CDK12 in standard genetic testing panels used to assess hereditary prostate cancer risk. These panels examine multiple genes associated with inherited cancer susceptibility, helping identify individuals who may benefit from closer medical monitoring.
Importantly, the clinical technology required to detect CDK12 mutations already exists. That could make expanding genetic testing relatively straightforward, potentially reducing the time and expense needed to bring the discovery into routine patient care.
"One of the most exciting aspects of this discovery is that we already have the technology needed to act on it," said Dr. Wyatt, who is also a senior research scientist at the Vancouver Prostate Centre and senior scientist at BC Cancer. "Adding CDK12 to existing genetic tests is relatively straightforward, which means this discovery could move from the research lab into clinical care much more quickly."
Could the Same Mutation Increase Ovarian Cancer Risk?
The study also uncovered clues suggesting that inherited CDK12 mutations might be associated with ovarian cancer, although more research is needed to establish whether they increase the risk.
Several of the men with inherited CDK12 mutations had relatives with a history of ovarian cancer. The investigators also identified another person who had ovarian cancer and carried an inherited CDK12 mutation. Analysis of that person's tumor revealed the same characteristic genetic signature seen in the prostate cancer cases.
Together, these observations suggest that CDK12 could potentially play a role in hereditary cancer risk beyond the prostate. Further studies will be needed to determine how strongly the mutations are associated with ovarian cancer and whether they should influence screening recommendations.
For families carrying these rare mutations, the potential benefits of identifying their genetic risk could be substantial. Earlier testing may give relatives the opportunity to receive closer surveillance and, if cancer develops, begin treatment before it reaches an advanced stage.
"With the right genetic testing and screening programs, we envision a future where no one who inherits one of these mutations dies from cancer," said Dr. Wyatt.
The research received funding from the Prostate Cancer Foundation, Terry Fox Research Institute, Canadian Cancer Society, Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Michael Smith Health Research BC, U.S. National Institutes of Health, BC Cancer Foundation, and other funding partners.

articles.title: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist
articles.text:
Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist
- Date:
- November 18, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- New research reveals that the brain makes free choices and forced decisions using surprisingly similar neural processes, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The discovery challenges assumptions about free will while suggesting that our personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose.
- Share:
Imagine you’re in line at your favorite bakery, deciding whether to have a doughnut or a tart. You weigh them up, the doughnut wins, and you settle on that.
By the time you’re at the front of the line, however, only tarts are left. So, you buy one.
These two decisions feel completely different. One involves deliberation based on our unique and personal preferences, while the other involves simply recognizing and picking the only available option.
But our latest research published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience shows our brains actually make these decisions in surprisingly similar ways.
What exactly is a free choice?
When we make free decisions, we recognize multiple options exist, weigh them up, and commit to one based on something internal: our preferences, values and goals.
Forced decisions are different. There’s only one possible outcome, and our job is simply to identify the option and take it.
Because free decisions feel so closely tied to who we are, neuroscientists have long assumed they rely on different processes in the brain compared to forced decisions. Some brain imaging studies support this, showing different patterns of neural activity distributed across the brain.
However, knowing where in the brain free choices happen tells us little about how they are formed – and whether this process is any different from forced decisions.
How does the brain form a decision?
Decades of research have shown that, to make decisions, our brains gradually gather evidence for each option over time.
Think of it like a judge evaluating the facts of a case. Once enough evidence has been accumulated in favour of one party, a verdict is reached. For some types of decisions, this happens very quickly (over hundreds of milliseconds), making it feel like the choice just popped into your head.
By measuring electrical brain activity, researchers have identified a brain signal that reflects this accumulation of evidence during simple decisions – such as judging whether a traffic light is red or green.
Like a loading bar building to 100%, the signal gradually rises to a particular level before a decision is made. Because the action of neurons in the brain is noisy, this decision-making process also occurs in a noisy fashion: rather than climbing steadily towards one option, the signal fluctuates back and forth between the alternatives.
This partly explains why we aren’t always consistent with our choices – even when our preferences are stable, some days we will go for the tart and others, the doughnut.
This signal has been identified for forced decisions with a clear correct answer. But what about choices that are open-ended – shaped not just by what’s in front of us, but by something internal like preferences or personal goals?
Tracing brain signals of decision formation
To answer this question, we recorded people’s brain activity while they chose between sets of colored balloons. They viewed either two balloons of different colors to freely choose between, or a single balloon they were forced to pick.
They pressed a button the moment they made their choice, and we tracked how brain activity unfolded in the lead-up to that moment.
For both free and forced decisions, the brain activity unfolded in a very similar way. Like a loading bar, it climbed steadily to the same peak level just before a choice was made. When people decided quickly, the signal increased faster. When they took longer, it rose more slowly.
That’s exactly what you would expect if the brain were tracking and weighing up evidence over time, rather than simply reacting to a decision at the last moment.
Does this mean our free choices aren’t really free?
From this finding, one might assume the brain forms free and forced decisions in the same way, suggesting decision-making in the brain may be more automatic than it feels.
This echoes famous experiments by neuroscientist Benjamin Libet in the 1980s. He and colleagues found brain activity begins ramping up before people are even consciously aware of their intention to act – suggesting the brain has already begun deciding before the person consciously realizes they’ve made a choice.
But while the process may be automatic, what the brain is accumulating tells a different story. The evidence it weighs up is drawn entirely from who you are – your preferences, your goals, your experiences. Two people may go through the same neural process and land on the same choice, and yet arrive there for completely different reasons.
So rather than asking whether our choices are truly free, perhaps the better question is what it really means for a choice to be yours. And the next time you find yourself in line at the bakery, know that your brain has already been quietly gathering evidence toward your baked good of choice, and that choice happens a little faster than you realize.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lauren C. Fong, Paul M. Garrett, Philip L. Smith, Robert Hester, Stefan Bode, Daniel Feuerriegel. Tracing the neural trajectories of evidence accumulation and motor preparation processes during voluntary decisions. Imaging Neuroscience, 2026; 4 DOI: 10.1162/IMAG.a.1184

articles.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
articles.text:
This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
- Date:
- November 18, 2026
- Source:
- Field Museum
- Summary:
- More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.
- Share:
A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared. The strange animal, an early relative of modern amphibians, has also received a name with a personal connection to the two student scientists who helped identify it.
During the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different. Instead of a modern city, the landscape was a warm, swampy river delta populated by giant insects, early animals adapted to life on land, and unusual creatures swimming through its waterways. This environment supported an extraordinary variety of life, leaving behind fossils that now provide a remarkable glimpse into Earth's prehistoric past.
The newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog. Its name means "Jean's crawler from Mazon Creek," honoring the mothers of the two student researchers, both of whom are named Jean. The discovery is described in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.
A 309-Million-Year-Old Fossil With Extraordinary Detail
The Mazon Creek fossil deposits are among the world's most important sources of Carboniferous fossils, in large part because of the conditions that existed when the animals were alive.
As plants and animals died in the ancient river delta, layers of sediment quickly covered their remains. This rapid burial created ideal conditions for fossilization, sometimes preserving delicate structures that would ordinarily disappear long before they could become fossils.
"What's really cool about Mazon Creek is that it preserves all of these unusual details -- things like toe pads and body outlines," says Allison Sefcovic, co-lead author of the paper and 2025 Women in Science intern at the Field.
"In the fossil of Jeanerpeton, we can see some of the scales on its back and tiny 'belly ribs' called gastralia. You can even see the eye impressions! It's so cool to see."
These exceptionally preserved features offer valuable evidence of what early amphibian relatives looked like. They also indicate that several anatomical characteristics associated with modern frogs and salamanders were already present approximately 309 million years ago.
A Prehistoric Species Hidden in Plain Sight
Although Jeanerpeton mazonensis has only recently been formally described, its fossil was discovered many years earlier. An amateur fossil collector originally found the specimen and later donated it to the Field Museum.
When researchers first examined it, they classified the animal as Amphibamus grandiceps, a previously established species known from the Mazon Creek area. However, closer examination eventually revealed that the fossil represented a distinct animal.
Misidentifications like this can occur when scientists have limited information about ancient species. Fossils that appear similar are sometimes assigned to an existing species even when important differences have not yet been recognized.
Paleontologists refer to such broad classifications as a "waste bin taxon." The term describes a category in which multiple fossils are grouped together because they seem related, even though their true identities and evolutionary relationships remain poorly understood.
"What we're finding from the Field Museum's collection are a bunch of things that historically were grouped together into this waste bin taxon known as Amphibamus grandiceps," says Cam So, co-author on the study and postdoctoral researcher at the Field Museum.
"Jeanerpeton is one of those species. And now, we've found enough evidence to support it being an anatomically distinct animal. With this publication, we officially pull Jeanerpeton out of this waste bin taxon."
The finding highlights how museum collections can continue to produce discoveries long after fossils are first collected. In this case, a specimen already held by the Field Museum provided enough anatomical evidence to establish a separate species.
Two Student Scientists Make a Remarkable Discovery
The research was co-led by Payton Kohlberg and Allison Sefcovic, who participated in the Field Museum's Women in Science internship program in 2025. The initiative encourages young women to explore careers in scientific research and museums.
Both students worked alongside So as members of the research group led by Arjan Mann, the museum's assistant curator of fossil fishes and early tetrapods in the Negaunee Integrative Research Center.
For Kohlberg, the project offered an opportunity to enter an unfamiliar scientific field and gain confidence through hands-on research.
"Before working in the Mann Lab, I didn't know much about paleontology," says Kohlberg. "My experience at the Field and in the Women in Science program has made me more confident in my abilities to try something new. It is scary to take on a project when you feel like you don't know as much as you should, but I learned with my practical experience that it is possible to overcome that fear with hard work."
The identification of Jeanerpeton mazonensis adds another species to the growing record of ancient life preserved at Mazon Creek. As researchers continue examining fossils from the region, each discovery helps reveal more about the extraordinary diversity of animals and plants that inhabited Illinois more than 300 million years ago.

articles.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
articles.text:
Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
- Date:
- November 18, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.
- Share:
Exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance. New research suggests that excessive training can also disrupt brain chemistry, potentially interfering with the processes that help the brain return to its normal resting state.
In a new study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.
The scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering. Dopamine plays an important role in motivation and alertness, and the researchers believe that similar disruptions in humans could help explain why excessive training is sometimes associated with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue. If confirmed, this connection would provide further evidence that sufficient rest is essential for both physical fitness and mental well-being.
"Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain," said Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study's first author.
Rocha carried out the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP) in Brazil, supported by a scholarship from FAPESP. He explained that the findings demonstrate how exercise influences the central nervous system, with effects extending well beyond muscle development.
How Scientists Simulated Overtraining
To investigate what happens in the brain when exercise becomes excessive, the team studied two main groups of mice exposed to different levels of physical activity.
One group completed a single strenuous treadmill session, running until they reached exhaustion. The other followed an extended training program designed to reproduce the demanding conditions associated with overtraining syndrome in elite athletes.
Overtraining syndrome occurs when the physical demands of training exceed the body's ability to recover. It can cause declining athletic performance, reduced appetite, ongoing fatigue, muscle pain, and a greater risk of injuries. Changes in immune function and metabolism are also common.
For the extended training experiment, the mice exercised over eight weeks as the researchers gradually increased the workload. By the final week, they were completing two sessions each day, with only four hours of recovery between workouts.
After the exercise programs, the scientists examined the animals' hippocampi. They measured dopamine and serotonin, along with proteins involved in producing and managing these chemical messengers. These included tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme needed for dopamine production, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), which helps package neurotransmitters for release.
Dopamine Remained Elevated for 48 Hours
In mice that completed just one exhausting treadmill session, dopamine levels increased shortly after exercise. This showed that even a single bout of intense activity could produce a measurable chemical response in the brain.
The more striking results came from the animals that underwent weeks of demanding training. In this group, both dopamine and TyrH remained elevated for 48 hours after the performance test, even though the mice were in their recovery period.
This prolonged response suggests that repeated strenuous exercise without sufficient rest may interfere with the brain's normal regulation of dopamine. Rather than quickly returning to its usual chemical state, the brain continued to show signs of altered neurotransmitter activity long after the exercise had ended.
Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, explained that finding comparable changes in humans could help researchers better understand the possible connections between overtraining, brain chemistry, and sleep disturbances.
However, the researchers caution that the study did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness. Those possible consequences remain to be investigated, and additional research is needed to determine whether the same dopamine changes occur in people.
Why Dopamine Balance Matters
Dopamine is often associated with pleasure and motivation, but it also helps regulate wakefulness and other essential brain functions. Its presence is not harmful on its own. What matters is whether its activity remains appropriately balanced.
According to Rocha, difficulties could arise if dopamine remains unusually elevated when the brain should be preparing for sleep. Such changes could also disrupt the balance between dopamine and other neurotransmitters, potentially affecting how the nervous system regulates activity and rest.
Another notable finding involved serotonin, a neurotransmitter that has long been investigated for its possible role in fatigue. Despite the substantial changes in dopamine, the researchers detected no significant differences in serotonin levels between the animals.
This result challenges the long-standing idea that serotonin alone is primarily responsible for excessive fatigue. Instead, the findings suggest that changes in dopamine regulation may also deserve attention when scientists investigate the biological effects of overtraining.
Why Recovery Is Essential for the Brain and Body
Although the connection between these chemical changes and symptoms such as insomnia or anxiety has not yet been established in humans, the findings reinforce the importance of allowing sufficient time for recovery.
Excessive training without adequate rest can undermine the benefits of exercise, contributing to reduced performance, persistent muscle pain, and problems with immune function. The new results suggest that changes in brain chemistry may be another important part of this process.
For recreational exercisers and professional athletes alike, the researchers emphasize that training should be balanced with appropriate recovery and expert guidance. Increasing workout intensity does not necessarily produce better results if the body is not given enough time to adapt.
Rocha also conducted research during a postdoctoral fellowship at the School of Applied Sciences (FCA) of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) in Limeira. This work included an internship at the University of Michigan in the United States, where he currently works as a researcher.
Additional funding came from a Thematic Project led by Silva, a postdoctoral fellowship awarded to Ana Paula Pinto, and a direct doctorate scholarship supporting João Pedro Floriano. Both Pinto and Floriano are affiliated with EEFERP-USP.
The team is now participating in a new international research project aimed at identifying which biological systems first begin to show signs of strain when exercise exceeds the level at which it normally produces beneficial adaptations. Understanding these early warning signals could help scientists determine when productive training begins to become harmful.

articles.title: A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system
articles.text:
A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system
- Date:
- November 18, 2026
- Source:
- Garvan Institute of Medical Research
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that a rare, potentially life-threatening inflammatory disorder is driven by malfunctioning immune cells, overturning three decades of scientific understanding. The breakthrough points to a promising new treatment using existing medications, with one severely affected infant already showing substantial improvement.
- Share:
For decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder. Now, researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have uncovered evidence that challenges 30 years of established thinking and could open the door to a new treatment.
The condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening. A new study published in Immunity identifies a previously underrecognized problem involving natural killer (NK) cells, immune cells that normally help the body eliminate infected cells.
The researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur. The discovery also points to a possible treatment using existing medications called JAK inhibitors, which could be particularly valuable for patients who do not respond to current therapies.
"This study has revealed a new target for this inflammatory disorder and sets the scene for future clinical studies to explore the use of JAK inhibitors or other drugs to neutralize interferon gamma in patients with MKD," says Professor Mike Rogers, Lab Head at Garvan and senior author of the study. "This could lead to a targeted treatment that hasn't been tried before."
Why a Rare Immune Disease Causes Dangerous Inflammation
MKD is a lifelong condition known to affect hundreds of children and adults around the world, although researchers suspect that many people with the disorder have never been diagnosed. Patients experience recurring attacks of high fever, skin rashes, joint pain, and inflammation in the abdomen. The most serious episodes can cause potentially fatal complications.
For roughly three decades, research into the disease has largely centered on macrophages, immune cells that help coordinate the body's inflammatory defenses. Existing treatments are designed to block an inflammatory signal released by these cells. However, approximately half of patients do not respond adequately, leaving a major need for better treatment options.
To investigate what might be missing from the prevailing explanation, the Garvan team examined blood samples from people with MKD and studied preclinical models of the disorder.
Their experiments revealed a significant defect in natural killer cells, which play an important role in the body's early defenses against viral infections. In MKD, these cells fail to mature properly and struggle to perform one of their most important functions: destroying infected cells before an infection can spread.
The consequences go beyond an impaired ability to fight infection. When natural killer cells cannot eliminate their targets, they release large amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, activating other parts of the immune system and potentially triggering widespread inflammation.
"We found that these immune cells are essentially misfiring," explains Professor Rogers. "NK cells are loaded with toxic ammunition, stored in granules that are released to kill infected cells. However, in MKD these toxic granules can't be released from NK cells and remain trapped inside. When an NK cell fails to kill its target, it compensates by shouting for help, pumping out large amounts of interferon gamma - a powerful inflammatory signal. This activates other immune cells and causes the dangerous fever and widespread inflammation seen in patients."
Discovery Challenges 30 Years of Immune Disease Research
The findings suggest that natural killer cell dysfunction, rather than macrophage activity alone, plays a central role in driving MKD.
Dr. Marcia Munoz, Group Leader in the Rogers Lab and lead researcher on the study, says the results represent a major change in how scientists understand the disease.
"This really turns on its head 30 years of dogma about what was thought to be the underlying mechanism of disease. In MKD, the primary problem is in NK cells and not in macrophages, as previously believed," she says.
To investigate how this cellular defect contributes to the disorder, the Garvan researchers collaborated with Professor Mariapia Degli-Esposti and scientists at Monash University.
Using preclinical models, the team established a connection between malfunctioning natural killer cells and the severe symptoms associated with MKD. Their experiments showed that when the immune system cannot clear a viral infection, the resulting inflammatory response can cause extensive damage to organs.
These results help explain why a disorder involving defective immune defenses can also produce episodes of extreme inflammation.
Existing Drug Shows Promise for a New Treatment
The discovery has already helped guide an experimental treatment approach for a severely affected infant.
Working with doctors at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, the researchers explored whether baricitinib could reduce the excessive inflammatory signaling associated with MKD.
Baricitinib belongs to a class of medications known as JAK inhibitors. These drugs interfere with signaling pathways used by the immune system, including those involved in responses to interferon gamma. The medication is already used to treat other immune-related conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and eczema.
Doctors added baricitinib to the infant's existing treatment regimen and subsequently observed an improvement in the child's condition. Inflammatory flare-ups became less frequent, and severe inflammation affecting the gastrointestinal tract began to heal.
Although the results from a single patient cannot establish whether the treatment will work more broadly, the improvement provides encouraging early evidence for a strategy that targets a different part of the inflammatory process.
The researchers believe their findings provide a foundation for future clinical studies investigating JAK inhibitors and other medications that block interferon gamma activity in patients with MKD, particularly those who have not benefited from standard treatments.
Discovery Could Help Explain Other Genetic Diseases
The potential implications extend beyond MKD itself.
Researchers have introduced the term 'prenylopathies' to describe a family of genetic disorders involving the same metabolic pathway affected in MKD. Early findings suggest that these related diseases may share a similar underlying problem involving natural killer cells that fail to function properly and instead generate excessive inflammatory signals.
If further studies confirm this connection, scientists may be able to identify common disease mechanisms and develop more targeted approaches to diagnosis and treatment across multiple disorders.
"Confirming this link could help end the diagnostic odyssey many patients endure for years or even decades before receiving effective treatment," says Professor Rogers.
Professor Mike Rogers is a Conjoint Professor at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney. Dr. Marcia Munoz is a Conjoint Senior Lecturer at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney.

articles.title: Scientists create a remarkable new rechargeable battery using vitamin B12
articles.text:
Scientists create a remarkable new rechargeable battery using vitamin B12
- Date:
- November 18, 2026
- Source:
- University of Córdoba
- Summary:
- Scientists have found a surprising new use for vitamin B12, developing a rechargeable battery that uses the essential nutrient to help generate and store electricity. The prototype survived up to 250 charging cycles and could open the door to safer, cheaper, and more environmentally friendly alternatives to lithium-ion batteries.
- Share:
Scientists have found an unexpected new use for vitamin B12, a nutrient best known for its importance to human health. Researchers at the University of Córdoba have incorporated the vitamin into a rechargeable battery, demonstrating for the first time that it can serve as a catalyst in this type of energy storage system.
Vitamin B12 is essential for normal bodily function and is naturally present in animal products. The vitamin is produced by certain bacteria, which occur in nature and are also grown commercially to supply the food and pharmaceutical industries. In addition to its established applications in medicine, nutrition, and veterinary care, B12 is used to address certain nutritional deficiencies. It has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because of its potential to help reduce fatigue.
Now, scientists are exploring an entirely different application. By using the vitamin to support the chemical reactions inside a battery, they have developed a prototype capable of completing up to 250 charging and discharging cycles.
How Vitamin B12 Makes a Rechargeable Battery Possible
The new battery was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba's Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). It uses zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air to produce electricity, with vitamin B12, also called cobalamin, playing a crucial role in the process.
To make the design work, the researchers attached vitamin B12 molecules to single-walled carbon nanotubes. The vitamin contains cobalt (III) at its center, which helps drive the electrochemical reactions needed for the battery to function.
The team has previously experimented with natural molecules as battery catalysts, including hemoglobin and catalase. These substances contain iron (II) and iron (III), respectively. Vitamin B12 represents the group's third effort to use a biological molecule for this purpose, but it has delivered an important advance: a battery that can be recharged repeatedly, completing as many as 250 cycles.
One of the biggest obstacles was keeping vitamin B12 inside the battery. Because the vitamin dissolves readily in water, it would normally be difficult to retain in a system that relies on a water-based electrolyte.
The researchers overcame this problem by securing the vitamin to carbon nanotubes, using an approach inspired by how amino acids connect to form proteins.
Manuel Cano Luna, one of the study's authors, explained that "we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in new batteries," while describing the team's search for useful biological compounds.
Their attachment technique imitates "the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins."
Alongside Cano Luna, the research team included Valentín García Caballero, Miguel López León, Pablo Gómez Argudo, Luis Camacho Delgado, José Miguel Rodríguez Mellado, María Teresa Martín Romero, José Abad López, and Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero.
A Safer, Lighter Alternative to Lithium-Ion Batteries
The findings, published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A, could contribute to the development of battery technologies that depend less on the materials used in conventional lithium-ion batteries.
Although lithium-ion batteries are widely used, obtaining their raw materials can involve significant economic, environmental, and social challenges. Zinc-air batteries offer a potential alternative because they can store substantial amounts of energy relative to their weight while relying on materials that are more readily available.
Zinc is abundant and recyclable, and these batteries use oxygen from the surrounding atmosphere as part of their energy-producing reactions. Because they draw oxygen from the air rather than storing all the necessary reactants internally, they can also be lighter than other battery designs.
This advantage has helped make zinc-air batteries increasingly useful in compact electronic devices, particularly hearing aids. Another benefit is their use of non-flammable, water-based electrolytes, which can reduce fire risks and improve safety.
Why Vitamin B12 Is Key to Recharging
A major challenge in developing rechargeable zinc-air batteries is finding a catalyst that can efficiently support the chemical reactions involved in both producing and storing electricity.
During discharge, the battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Recharging requires the relevant chemical reactions to proceed in the opposite direction. A suitable catalyst must therefore be effective in both processes.
According to researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero, vitamin B12 "has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen."
This ability to support both reactions is what makes the vitamin particularly promising for rechargeable zinc-air battery technology.
Could Vitamin B12 Help Store Renewable Energy?
The successful prototype offers a new direction for researchers seeking affordable, sustainable alternatives to existing energy storage technologies.
If the approach can be developed further, batteries using vitamin B12 catalysts could eventually help address one of the biggest challenges facing renewable energy: storing excess electricity generated by sources such as solar and wind power for use when production falls.
Although the technology remains at the research stage, demonstrating up to 250 charge and discharge cycles shows that a familiar biological molecule can play an unexpected role in rechargeable battery design. The discovery adds to growing efforts to use naturally occurring substances to create safer, lighter, and more sustainable ways to store energy.
